title: A/B Testing and the Two-Party Trap
intro: Calabro compares A/B testing to the US two-party system: both assume almost any problem reduces to two options, and both sell clarity while delivering a narrow answer.

topics.title: A/B Testing and the Two-Party Trap

learn.title: The false choice
learn.text:
An A/B test only compares the two things you thought of. Life doesn't work that way: users, like voters, aren't a toggle. They are driven by a network of motivations, needs and context.

A user might like option A's interaction and option B's layout. A binary test has no way to say so.

try.q: Variant B beat variant A. What have you learned?
options: B did better than A on that metric
B is the best possible design for users
Users understand and like variant B
The redesign as a whole was worth doing
try.explain: Winning a two-way comparison says nothing about options you didn't test, or why B won.

learn.title: The illusion of learning
learn.text:
A/B testing promises hard data on which design is better. But you are looking at **one variable at a time**.

“You might get a 5% bump in clicks by changing a button size, but what does that really tell you about the overall experience?”

try.q: A bigger button gets 5% more clicks. What does Calabro say this tells you about the overall experience?
options: Very little
That the page is now easier to use
That users prefer larger controls
That conversion will rise by 5% too
try.explain: One variable on one metric is a narrow answer.

learn.title: Confounds, and what to do
learn.text:
Test more than one element at once, such as button placement and navigation structure, and you can no longer tell which change caused the result.

Factors interact. That is why Calabro prefers **multivariate testing** when several things change, plus research that explains why.

try.q: You change the button placement and the navigation in the same A/B variant, and it wins. What is the problem?
options: You can't tell which change caused the result
The sample was too small to be valid
A/B tests can't measure changes to navigation structure
Winning variants must always be re-tested
try.explain: Two changes in one variant are confounded.

test.q: What do A/B testing and a two-party system share, in Calabro's analogy?
options: They reduce complex choices to two options
They both rely on very large samples
They always produce a clear majority
They measure opinions rather than behaviour
test.explain: Both squeeze real-world complexity into an artificial binary.

test.q: What can a binary test not express?
options: Liking parts of A and parts of B
Which variant got more clicks
A difference in conversion rate
That one option lost the comparison
test.explain: Anything that doesn't fit the two options is ignored.

test.q: What does Calabro recommend when several factors interact?
options: Multivariate testing
Running the same A/B test twice
Testing with a smaller audience
Asking stakeholders to pick a winner
test.explain: It accounts for how different factors shape behaviour together.

test.q: Why is the “clarity” of an A/B result limited?
options: It looks at one variable at a time
It can only be run on mobile traffic
It never reaches significance
It needs users to explain their choice
test.explain: A narrow comparison gives a narrow answer.

test.q: Which statement fits the article best?
options: It compares two options; it doesn't show either is good
A/B tests are useless and should be dropped
A/B tests are reliable only for small visual changes to a page
A/B results should always override research
test.explain: It is a critique of binary thinking, not a ban on testing.
